title: Smarter trial footprints: what we heard at our ESMO 2026 roundtable
body_markdown:
At ESMO 2026, the science gave us plenty to celebrate. We saw strong data from mRNA vaccines, bispecific antibodies and ADCs. But as our roundtable moderator Luca Cantini put it, many patients still don’t have access to clinical trials.


That gap shaped our roundtable in Madrid on 25 October. We brought together biotech, biopharma, patient advocacy and Fortrea around one question: how can we make better trial placement decisions that reduce execution risk and reach more patients?


## 1. The bottleneck has shifted from science to access


The science is getting more precise. The harder problem now is finding, reaching and enrolling the right patients in the right places. Where a patient lives still has a big say in whether they can join a trial.


## 2. Placement is an investment decision


Sponsors with resource constraints have to weigh several things when choosing countries: how many eligible patients there are, how capable the sites are, speed, cost and risk. We discussed mature markets such as the US and Australia alongside evolving ones such as India and LATAM. The point was not that one group is better. Expanding into a new market works when it’s planned deliberately, with protocol-specific access and capable sites.


## 3. Finding a patient is only the first step


The patient advocacy view was clear. Even when the data shows an eligible patient exists, the system can still miss them. Biomarker testing, referral pathways, navigation and practical support are what turn awareness into enrollment.


## 4. Use data to sharpen decisions, not replace judgement


AI-enabled feasibility and recruitment data can make country and site comparisons faster and more transparent. Specialist judgement on protocol fit and site readiness still matters.


## Principles to take forward


- Bring data, patient and delivery stakeholders in before country assumptions are locked.
- Keep feasibility assumptions visible through study start-up and recruitment.
- Track the whole journey, from the first sign of an eligible patient to screening and enrollment.
- Enter new geographies with local evidence and patient-support pathways in place.
- Use collaborations to join up the ecosystem, not to add fragmented hand-offs.


## Continuing the conversation


The roundtable ended on a question we keep coming back to. At ESMO 2030, will success be defined by the next breakthrough, or by how many patients could actually access it?


We would like to keep that conversation going.
